newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea to relax probes into funding sources.
newsitem.headline: South Korea to relax probes into funding sources.

text.p: South Korea's finance minister said on Tuesday probes into sources of funds would be relaxed to bring underground money into the economy.
Minister Kang Kyong-shik told reporters the government would also push legislation banning money laundering to prevent corruption and accumulation of slush funds.
These steps were part of a package that the finance ministry disclosed to improve the real-name financial system, which bans the use of false names in all financial transactions.
"In principle, funds converted into real-name accounts would not be tracked," Kang said.
He said his ministry would not investigate the source of money if it is reported to tax authorities and deposited into real-name accounts.
Currently, financial authorities are required to investigate bank account holders who move more than 200 million won ($227,000) into a real-name account from a false-name account.
"We plan to complete the legislation of the revision as early as possible, even before the regular session of the National Assembly," Kang said.
The plenary session usually opens in September.

As part of the package, small companies would be exempted from probes into funding sources even if the funds are from a false-name account, Kang said. Funds used for the launching and the capital increase of small firms and venture companies would receive the same treatment.
The real-name financial system was introduced in 1993 to root out corruption and force underground money into the economic system.
But the system has been criticised for causing bottlenecks in the economy as fears of tax probes and audits drove underground money into a deeper closet.
The Korea Tax Institute's report showed the underground economy had not shrunk since the introduction of the system.
It accounted for 8.9 percent of the nation's gross national product in 1995 from 8.7 percent in 1993, the report showed.
Kang also said the revision would be carried out in a way as not to destroy the basic principle of the real-name financial system.

Ministry officials said the ministry was not considering allowing false-name trading of long-term bonds issued to raise funds for infrastructure projects, as had been rumoured in local financial markets.
"Such bond trading is unlikely because that means the complete surrender to the old practice of dubious financial transactions," said a ministry official.
On Monday President Kim Young-sam urged Kang to leave intact the basic principles of the financial transaction system.
When Kang was appointed new minister earlier this month, he told reporters he would review the real-name system as the first step to revive the sagging economy.
"Kang's plans showed some improvement," said Lee Hahn-ku, president of the Daewoo Research Institute. "We can expect more blackmarket money to flow into the banking system."
